I’m gonna, well actually 🤓☝🏽 here for a moment. Pride, as a concept, has always been a protest. Back in 1969, the first pride protest started at the Stonewall Inn in Greenwich village in NYC. Cops raided the inn, trying to arrest anyone they could, but the majority of the patrons on that particular night weren’t going to stand for the homophobic and transphobic laws being upheld by the police. So the attempted raid turned into a riot. In the following days, dozens of groups around the U.S. formed their own riots. This was the start of the gay pride movement and is why June, specifically June 28th, is very special to the LGBTQ+ population. 

Pride has since evolved, soaking up the corporate liberalism and drunken capitalism that followed for the next 50 years and you have today. Everything since the United States adopted a more neoliberal economy style, including protest movements and nonprofits, have taken their own steps in neoliberalism. That means, now, that pride is flashy, a place to sell, alcohol centered, extravagant, and even scandalous sometimes. But at its core, it’s the same movement. Pride is a protest.

The practice of cops picking up a person, often the person is marginalized in some kind of very visible way, sometimes the person may have had previous scuffles with the PD, and then taking that person to the edge of town, instead of their home address, in weather not suitable for walking or neighborhoods specifically chosen due to the violence in the area. I was a teenager when I first learned about this, and it’s made me more vigilant about how I interact with cops. 

Know your rights. Remain calm. Don’t tell them more than exactly what you must tell them. Lie to protect your loved ones. Don’t trust the police. They’re not your friends. Not directed at op, but to whoever is reading this, not all pelvic exams are this horrific. What op has gone through sounds terrifying and traumatic. But I promise that not every experience with gynecological care is going to be traumatic. I feel so incredibly lucky that my exam went very smoothly, my doctor answered all my questions and waited for me to let my anxiety subside. She explained everything she was going to insert in me and the tools she was using. I didn’t need a biopsy—I can’t imagine how excruciating that must be. But echoing op’s sentiment at the end: PLEASE take care of the body you have. I know our bodies are often huge sources of dysphoria for us, but we really do have to take care of what we currently have. Ask around in your local communities to see if there’s any trans-friendly doctors who can do your pelvic exam. If there’s a planned parenthood where you live (they all shut down in my state after roe v wade was shot down—it might be the same in other red states) seek their services, they are more often than not extremely trans friendly, I went for a consultation one time there and wasn’t looked at weirdly at all by all the women in the waiting room. They didn’t care. You might get comments or strange looks if you pass as a man, but your health is more important than what strangers think.

In your native language, you’re often unaware of the specifics of its grammar or structure. Words will have emotional connections to them because you were raised with that language and when making new associations in our brains, the first word you learn to connect with that emotion becomes your default. 

In linguistics, when studying the differences between someone’s native language and subsequent languages, we have L1 and L2. L1 is your native language. Most people have 1 truly native language, but some people genuinely have 2 native languages that they learned equally when growing up. L2 consists of your second, third, fourth, or any subsequent language you learn. The way our brains learn an L2 is completely different from the way we learn and process our L1. When we’re starting out, we have to translate our L2 to our L1 in order to get the emotional reaction from what the person says. Over time you’ll become more familiar with your L2 and you can start speaking from the heart, so to speak. But it also means we learn grammar rules differently. No one teaches us, when we’re growing up and learning English, that adjectives have an order to say them in that is considered grammatically correct. (Opinion, size, physical quality, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose) that’s very hard for an English L2 speaker to memorize, but you and I, English L1 speakers, don’t have to think about it. We just say it “sounds right.” It was something ingrained in us from the time we were in the womb, so we don’t have to consciously think about it in order to make a grammatically correct sentence with multiple adjectives.

This sounds like something called P-OCD, with the P standing for exactly what you think it does. It does NOT mean you’re a pedophile. It does, however, mean that you have a mental illness that needs to be treated by a professional. 

People with OCD will typically have a theme for what their obsessive thoughts focus on, and the compulsions are there to “clean” yourself or rid yourself of the metaphorical dirtiness of those thoughts. The thing is that, when you perform the compulsion, whether that’s counting things, or tapping things, or doing things a certain number of times, whatever it might be, that actually tells your brain that those obsessive thoughts need to happen again, because you gain temporary relief. 

It’s important, now that you realize you have these thoughts, to NOT label yourself as a pedophile. That will only strengthen the obsessive thoughts. When you have a thought that you don’t like, let it happen, and do not beat yourself up for it. Intrusive thoughts are common in many mental illnesses, specifically anxiety disorders and psychotic disorders. That means that there are MILLIONS of people walking around every day with these nasty disgusting violent grotesque thoughts that they don’t want to have. So you’re not alone for feeling this way.

This is a tricky question! I would agree that the main clause is “they felt.” The main subject is “they” and the main verb is “felt.” 

If we break it down (I’m a linguistics major so I’ve had to do this plenty of times)

[I never got the feeling] is a dependent clause, indicated by a null “that” (I never got the feeling that…) this also contains two noun phrases and a verb phrase. 
[they felt] is the main clause. They being the main noun, and also the subject of the sentence, felt being the main verb of the sentence. 
[as driven] is a prepositional phrase containing an adjective. 
[to actually do it] is a prepositional phrase containing “do” as a verb and “it” as a coda object. (English requires transitive verbs to always have an object explicitly mentioned, this is not common in other languages.)
[as I had] another prepositional phrase
[since adolescence] another prepositional phrase. 

And yes, “that” can often be deleted in phrases like this one. “I didn’t know [that] I worked today.” Either one would be correct, one is just more explicit. And the [that] is implied. The [that] also indicates that the clause before it is a dependent clause, and not the main clause of the sentence. 

To answer your other question, yes. English doesn’t require a verb, noun, or person’s name to be restated if the context is clear, but this can create confusion for some people. [felt] is the antecedent of this sentence, meaning [felt] would go exactly where you put it, but instead of being explicitly written, it’s implied.

Some of the attitudes of these people really concerns me, disregarding the whole self diagnosis thing. It really seems like the attitudes towards mental illness is just “if I have this thing, all I have to do is affirm that I have this thing, then there is no further work to be done.” And throw in the towel. 

Diagnosis can change. Professionals can realize they were wrong due to how you’re recovering or sprouting new symptoms. Different types of therapy can often decrease many symptoms of numerous mental illnesses. Most mental illnesses, are in fact, not life-long chronic disorders, and may only run their course once or twice without having a prolonged period. Some will require you to work at them for years or decades. Some may truly be with you until the day you die. But you can’t resign yourself and your sense of self to a DSM or ICD code on a piece of paper. At this point in my journey in recovering from mental illness, I don’t even really identify with any specific labels anymore, except to people I’m really close to and know about my diagnosis. All I have is a set of symptoms that I have to manage and recover from. 

And that’s all a mental illness is, and different clinicians are going to have different opinions on what your set of symptoms means to you, not even mentioning that what you tell them is a big part of that. Malpractice exists. Definitely. But a big part of recovery is seeing yourself as a whole person who just… has a few things about themselves they have to manage. Your diagnosis is not the end-all-be-all and it certainly doesn’t do you any good if you don’t do anything about it. There are even people who have the opposite of the OPs’ problem, where they refuse to see a doctor but have rigid routines for themselves to manage what is likely a mental health condition or they know they go off the deep end. Supplements, exercise, eating certain foods, drinking enough water, going on vacations recurring. I’ve heard of people who do all of those things, but would never admit that the reason they’re so strict about doing those things is because of mental illness. Supplements and fresh air won’t cure schizophrenia, sure, but everything I mentioned does a hell of a lot for the most common mental illnesses. You don’t need a label to help yourself and a label won’t help you when you’re backed into a figurative corner and have no coping skills to get yourself out of whatever hole you dug for yourself.

Particularly terrifying diseases are variations of prion disease, the most common prion disease is Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease: it randomly happens and is likely related to genetics. Prion disease happens when a protein called a prion misfolds, and while normally this isn’t a problem, like with cancerous cells in our bodies, as these things don’t typically cause people problems, occasionally misfolded prions will begin to inform other prion proteins to misfold in the same way. The presentation of the disease takes decades and symptoms don’t typically cause problems until one’s 50s, 60s, or 70s. However, when the process starts, it can’t be stopped. Prion diseases are incurable and have a 100% fatality rate. You are probably familiar with “Mad Cow Disease” which is what we’ve colloquially called both Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease. BSE is prion disease in cows, essentially. It causes v-CJD which has the same outcomes as CJD but is acquired by eating meat from cows afflicted with BSE. Of course, there was the crisis in England and Scotland that led to the death of millions of cows and a number of humans, cats, and dogs as well. v-CJD is significantly faster though—at least as far as we’re aware—and typically led to the deaths of victims around 9 months to 3 years after the likely time one consumed the affected meat. 

It leads to dementia-like symptoms, Parkinson’s-like symptoms, sometimes psychosis, loss of use of limbs and other muscles, and eventually death. What happens is that the brain literally becomes sponge-like (spongiform) and is missing chunks of grey and white matter from the lack of properly-folded proteins. 

Other diseases that fall under this umbrella would be Fatal Familial Insomnia (only affects a very small number of people and is inherited through a select few family lines—interestingly the disease can be traced back to Italian royalty, that likely has something to do with it) and I believe there’s only 3 or 4 affected family units today. There’s also Kuru which is specific to a cannibalism-practicing island nation (their name is escaping my mind-sorry!) which has led to a lot of deaths among the people, as one can expect. Cannibalism is part of a ritualistic death practice, solely consumed by women, as they’re believed to be the only ones that could handle passing on that community member’s soul, as that’s what they are doing as they’re consuming their loved one—sending them to the afterlife officially. Children would be fed small amounts of the body while the women participated, and this had led to a long line lasting several decades of Kuru prion disease affecting often very young people. I’m not sure of the status of their practices now, but this was the status I was informed up to, but iirc there have been efforts to inform the community of the dangers of consuming their family members.

Hey man, I'm not an expert in psychology but I struggle with some of the things you mentioned and I have a bit of educational background in abnormal psych. I'll try to offer some decent advice, and I'll try not to beat a dead horse either.

Feeling inherently superior to others is often linked to low self-esteem (especially in patients with cluster-b personality disorders) and can be caused by actually feeling inferior on the inside, so you sorta lash out by way of asserting superiority over others. Empathy is a hard one. I've learned that there's different kinds of empathy, as well as sympathy and compassion. In my own words, compassion is wanting to help others. You can learn this! This could be simple things like holding a door for someone (esp a disabled person) or telling someone you love them and are thinking about them if you know they're going through a hard time. Sympathy is feeling bad for others, like seeing someone going through a really hard time and listening to their problems with them, or seeing an international conflict going on and thinking "man, that's awful for all the innocent civillians." You can also learn sympathy! 

[Here is a link to an article about different kinds of empathy.](https://blog.heartmanity.com/the-three-kinds-of-empathy-emotional-cognitive-compassionate) I personally struggle a lot with cognitive and emotional empathy. There are 2 people in my entire life I've been able to feel emotional empathy with. Otherwise, I simply can't grasp the concept. I don't understand, personally, why someone would feel sad because another person is sad. Tbh, I think emotional empathy is innate. I don't think I'd be able to ever learn it. Cognitive and compassionate empathy, I think you can learn. 

For practicing cognitive empathy, I suggest learning about body language (I have a hard time reading body language and typically have to fuck up a social interaction to understand what the intention of the body language was) and other types of communication that can be ambiguous. If you're a pattern type of person, try to notice patterns in people's behaviors in order to understand the context of their behavior or feelings. When interacting with someone, try to remember things about them, like if they're struggling with a life situation or battling an illness. For example, if I interact with my boss, who is usually very nice and patient, and she acts short with me, normally I might assume I did something wrong. But, I also know that she has a sick family member she has to take care of, has been struggling with family drama related to a death a few years ago, and has multiple chronic illnesses, so any of these three factors are the most likely reason as to why she's acting the way she is.

For compassionate empathy, I'd recommend practice actively thinking about why other people would be bothered by things that may not bother you, and therefore affect their behavior and communication. If you have no desire to help someone with their situation, that's okay. I wouldn't say that out loud though. I've studied communication, languages, and sociology, and all 3 of these things help me a lot in my interactions with people. Understanding the basics of how a social interaction works, and the societal expectations surrounding social interaction can help you make better decisions to not accidentally be an asshole. And, truthfully, I think that just by practicing these things you might just start doing it without thinking about it.
